title: A Veil for the Wolf
premise: Oscar Reyes, a mercenary bound by an oath to the silent god Vael, has survived ten years in the Thornfell mountains by keeping her head down and her god's silence unexamined. When the old gods suddenly begin answering prayers — violently, selectively — she discovers her own oath-mark is the key: Vael did not die, he was imprisoned by the other gods, and his waking will either free the mountains from divine predation or ignite a war between the old pantheon and every mortal who ever swore to them. Hunted by the god-hunters of the Ashen Court and betrayed by the smuggler network that raised her, Oscar must choose between returning Vael to his prison (preserving a fragile peace built on lies) or breaking him loose and bearing the cost. She chooses freedom — and pays for it with her memories of everyone she loves, the price the old law demands — ending the war by becoming the living veil between gods and mortals.
about_author: J. M. Crane is the pen name of a former trail guide who spent five seasons in the northern ranges, writing at night by woodstove light. Known for morally tangled fantasy where the landscape is a character, Crane lives off-grid with two ill-tempered goats.

chapters.title: The Silence Owed
chapters.summary: Oscar Reyes escorts a pilgrim caravan through the Thornfell passes, trading on her knowledge of smuggler roads and the fading oath-mark on her wrist that no longer answers. When a shrine along the trail spontaneously ignites and the pilgrim's desperate prayer is answered with a miracle — and a death — Oscar realizes the silence is breaking. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: unease; the world she trusted is shifting under her boots.

chapters.title: Ashen Warrant
chapters.summary: The Ashen Court's god-hunters arrive in the border town of Greyhollow, executing anyone touched by answered prayer. Oscar hides a surviving child marked by the shrine-miracle, violating her mercenary neutrality for the first time in a decade. Her handler, the smuggler-queen Marisol, warns her to walk away. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: the first fracture in her careful detachment; she chooses a side without admitting it.

chapters.title: What the Mountain Remembers
chapters.summary: Guiding the marked child, Wren, into the deep passes, Oscar encounters a talking cairn — a minor god waking after centuries, half-mad, who recognizes her oath-mark and calls her 'Vael's key.' The cairn reveals Vael was not dead but bound, and that his silence was a prison, not abandonment. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: grief and fury; her decade of faithful abandonment was a lie.

chapters.title: The Price of the Mark
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter: ten years earlier, a younger Oscar swore her oath to Vael during the Saltmarsh Rebellion, believing she was buying her squad's survival. Only three of nine walked away, and she has never asked why. In the present, the mark begins burning as Vael stirs, feeding on her memories. POV: Oscar (dual timeline). Emotional beat: guilt surfacing; the past was never as clean as she told herself.

chapters.title: Hunters in the Pass
chapters.summary: The Ashen Court's chief hunter, Serah Vane, corners Oscar in a snowbound waystation. Vane offers a bargain: deliver Wren and the cairn-god's location, and the Court will erase her mark before Vael fully wakes. Oscar refuses and fights her way out, but Vane escapes knowing her face and name. POV: Oscar, with a closing Vane scene. Emotional beat: cold resolve hardening into open defiance.

chapters.title: The Smuggler's Ledger
chapters.summary: Oscar turns to Marisol's network for passage to Vael's prison-mountain, only to discover Marisol has already sold her out to the Court — the smuggler queen's own family died in the Saltmarsh, and she wants the old gods buried forever. Betrayed, Oscar escapes with Wren through the flooded mine-roads, losing her supplies and her last safe harbor. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: betrayal's bitter clarity; survival means trusting no one but the enemy god.

chapters.title: Prisoner of the Peak
chapters.summary: At the summit of Thornfell's highest peak, Oscar finds Vael's prison: not a cell but a marriage — he was bound into the mountain itself as part of an ancient truce, and waking him means unmaking the truce that ended the first divine war. Vael speaks to her at last, and he is not a savior; he is tired, angry, and honest about the cost. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: the seduction and terror of a truth with no clean exit.

chapters.title: Court of Knives and Prayers
chapters.summary: Vane's forces and Marisol's smugglers converge on the peak while the other waking old gods arrive to defend the truce. In the chaos, Wren — the marked child — is revealed to be the truce's living anchor, born to be sacrificed to reseal Vael if he wakes. Oscar must fight through both armies to reach her. POV: Oscar and Vane. Emotional beat: climax; every faction's justice demands a child's death, and Oscar refuses all of them.

chapters.title: The Breaking of the Veil
chapters.summary: Oscar breaks Vael's binding using her own oath-mark, offering the one payment the old law accepts: her memories. As gods and hunters battle around her, she recites the names of everyone she loves — Marisol, her dead squad, Wren — and lets the law take them, one by one. Vael wakes free, the truce shatters, and the old gods, facing a war they cannot win cheaply, withdraw. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: sacrificial climax; victory purchased with the self.

chapters.title: A Veil for the Wolf
chapters.summary: Weeks later, the passes are quiet. Oscar remembers nothing of her past — only skills, roads, and a name — but Vael walks beside her in mortal form, repaying his debt as her companion and witness. Wren, alive and unmarked, carries the memory of Oscar's sacrifice for her. Together they take the first contract offered: keeping the roads open between gods and mortals, so no prayer goes unanswered and no oath goes unpriced. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; a new life built on a foundation she can no longer see.
